Carbon fibers (CFs) embedded as short yarns in glass fabric composites can reduce radar cross section (RCS) via phase cancellation.
The proposed composites achieve more than 10 dB RCS reduction from 8.7 to 19.2 GHz with a thickness of 2.7 mm.
Two patterns studied are chessboard and random arrangements of CF yarn sub-regions on the composite surface.
The RCS reduction mechanism relies on creating a 180° phase difference between CF-loaded and pure glass fabric regions.
Short CF yarns are modeled as lossy cut-wire resonators with length 5.5 mm, width 1.0 mm, and thickness 0.06 mm.
The epoxy resin matrix is hardened by diethylenetriamine and reinforced with E-glass fabrics.
Permittivity of glass fabric composites is weakly frequency dispersive, measured from 8.2 to 12.4 GHz.
Electrical conductivity of CF yarns is assumed as 3.5×10^4 S/m longitudinally and 8.9×10^7 S/m transversely at 10 GHz.
Reflection measurements were performed in an anechoic chamber from 5.2 to 22 GHz under normal incidence.
Simulations show three resonant frequencies at approximately 8.8, 12.5, and 18.9 GHz with significant phase changes.
Maximum RCS reduction (>45 dB) occurs at 12.5 GHz for equal area fractions and reflection amplitudes.
Scattering contributes more to RCS reduction than absorption in these composites.
Defects removing up to ~6% of CF yarns cause only minor degradation in RCS reduction performance.
The composites can be extended to curved surfaces using non-planar pattern templates.
Fabrication uses needle punching and vacuum infusion techniques to embed CF yarns in glass fabric layers.
The proposed method avoids the need for additional functional fillers, maintaining mechanical properties.
The phase cancellation approach enables broadband RCS reduction beyond narrowband absorption methods.
The chessboard pattern produces distinct scattering beams, while the random pattern scatters more uniformly.
The study uses both analytical models and full-wave numerical simulations to design and predict performance.
